claim_as_stated: AI could eliminate up to half of entry-level white-collar jobs and push US unemployment to 10-20% within one to five years.
accuracy_rationale: graded: claim as made vs real-world outcome; deadline (2026-2030) has not arrived. As-made wording is faithfully hedged ('could', 'up to').
counterclaim_summary: Labor economists called it speculative and unsupported by current data; Acemoglu (Nobel 2024) called it motivated reasoning (2026-04). Amodei himself reframed via Jevons Paradox in 2026-05, retaining a disruption caveat.
counterclaimant: Daron Acemoglu; various economists; press analysis
notes: Dossier research 2026-07-07: named counterpoints and 2026 restatements recorded on the referent's references.

claim_as_stated: Generative AI is exposed to work equivalent to ~300 million full-time jobs globally; up to two-thirds of US/EU occupations exposed to some degree.
accuracy_rationale: graded: claim as made vs the report; faithful to the report's exposure framing. A restatement as '300M jobs will be lost' would grade mostly false.
counterclaim_summary: Exposure is tasks automatable/augmentable, not jobs lost; same report projects GDP gains.

claim_as_stated: About 40% of jobs worldwide are exposed to AI, ~60% in advanced economies, with roughly half of exposed jobs potentially harmed.
accuracy_rationale: graded: IMF's own wording vs its note; faithful, including the bidirectional 'exposure' and the 'half may benefit' caveat.
counterclaim_summary: IMF stressed ~half of exposed jobs could benefit; exposure is not displacement.

claim_as_stated: 40% of jobs are at risk from AI / will be lost to AI.
claim_source: Widely circulated paraphrase; not a specific named source
accuracy_rationale: graded: circulating phrasing vs the IMF source; swaps 'exposed' for 'at risk', drops that ~half may benefit. Not attributed to a named claimant here to avoid a fabricated attribution.
counterclaim_summary: The IMF source says exposed (bidirectional), not at risk.
verification_status: Distortion of a real source; example variant
notes: Included to demonstrate the referent/variant structure; unattributed on purpose.

claim_as_stated: By 2030, ~92 million jobs displaced and ~170 million created (net positive), with large gross churn.
accuracy_rationale: graded: forecast vs real-world outcome; a 2030 projection not yet testable. Faithful to the report as stated.
counterclaim_summary: Net effect framed positive; survey-based employer forecasts are unreliable predictors.

claim_as_stated: AI will make paid work optional; in the long run probably none of us will have a job.
claim_source: VivaTech / UK AI Safety Summit remarks
accuracy_rationale: graded: speculative claim vs outcome; no timeframe/mechanism, not testable.
counterclaim_summary: Widely regarded as long-horizon futurism.
notes: Exact venue/date of quote not pinned.

claim_as_stated: AI will write code at the level of a mid-level engineer; Meta may use AI for that work in 2025.
accuracy_rationale: graded: near-term prediction vs outcome; SWE employment had not collapsed as of the claim.
counterclaim_summary: Many argue AI augments developers and shifts the role rather than eliminating it.
notes: Episode reportedly 2025-01-10.

claim_as_stated: AI reduces the need to learn to code; everybody in the world is now a programmer.
accuracy_rationale: graded: claim as made vs its own reasoning; defensible as rhetoric about accessibility but misleads if read as 'coding skills are worthless'.
counterclaim_summary: Educators/engineers argue coding literacy still matters; AI shifts the work.
notes: Remarks reportedly 2024-02-12.

claim_as_stated: Generative AI could add trillions in value; half of today's work activities could be automated between ~2030 and 2060.
accuracy_rationale: graded: modeled long-range projection vs outcome; decades-long timeline not testable now. Faithful to the report as stated.
counterclaim_summary: MGI frames most impact as augmentation with heavy uncertainty.

claim_as_stated: AI will automate ~5% of tasks over ~10 years, with small productivity and GDP gains.
accuracy_rationale: graded: claim as made vs his own model; faithful to the paper's estimate and stated assumptions.
counterclaim_summary: AI-optimists argue this underestimates capability growth and compounding effects.

claim_as_stated: AI could help rebuild middle-skill, middle-class work by extending expertise to more workers.
accuracy_rationale: graded: claim as made vs real-world outcome; about an unrealized future. As-made wording is faithful to its own conditional framing.
counterclaim_summary: Skeptics argue the optimistic scenario depends on policy/deployment choices that may not materialize.
notes: If his stated mechanisms are pulled from the essay, they would attach here as subclaims (parent_claim_id=C010). None created without the source.

claim_as_stated: Employment declined for workers aged 22-25 in the most AI-exposed occupations, while older workers held up.
claim_source: 'Canaries in the Coal Mine?' working paper
accuracy_rationale: graded: claim as made vs the study; faithful, with the authors' own caution that it is early and correlational.
counterclaim_summary: Other factors (rates, post-pandemic normalization) may contribute.

claim_as_stated: Generative AI's measured effect on jobs and wages so far is minimal.
accuracy_rationale: graded: claim as made vs the study; faithful to its early-window finding.
counterclaim_summary: The window is early and may not capture later models.

claim_as_stated: AI-related displacement could drive large white-collar losses; the response should include a shorter work week.
accuracy_rationale: graded: forward-looking advocacy claim vs outcome; displacement scale not yet evidenced in aggregate data.
counterclaim_summary: Others argue gains/displacement are not yet large enough to justify the framing.

claim_as_stated: Studio use of AI threatens actors' and writers' livelihoods and likenesses, requiring consent and compensation protections.
accuracy_rationale: graded: the unions' stated position vs their bargaining record; faithful. Final contracts added AI guardrails.
counterclaim_summary: Studios argued AI could reduce costs and that some uses are complementary.

claim_as_stated: About 95% of enterprise generative-AI pilots show no measurable P&L impact.
accuracy_rationale: graded: claim as made vs the report; the report says this, but the headline 95% is contested and easily over-read as 'AI has no value'.
counterclaim_summary: Some analysts dispute the methodology and figure, arguing returns lag rather than being absent.

claim_as_stated: LLMs reproduce covert racial bias, judging African American English speakers more negatively even when overt bias appears reduced.
accuracy_rationale: graded: claim as made vs the study; faithful to its probing results.
counterclaim_summary: Some argue benchmark prompts do not reflect deployed safeguards; authors counter covert bias persists.

claim_as_stated: Generative image models amplify demographic stereotypes (high-status roles as white/male, lower-status as people of color).
accuracy_rationale: graded: claim as made vs the analysis; faithful to what they measured in the sampled outputs.
counterclaim_summary: Vendors add debiasing; over-correction can also distort (Gemini, 2024).

claim_as_stated: AI systems continue to encode discrimination and concentrate power; deployment without oversight risks systematic harm.
accuracy_rationale: graded: as a statement of her position vs her body of talks; faithful. (Position, not a single empirical result.)
counterclaim_summary: Some argue bias is measurable and improvable via engineering; dispute is on pace/adequacy.

claim_as_stated: Facial and generative systems carry documented biases; oversight and awareness of 'the coded gaze' are needed.
accuracy_rationale: graded: claim as made vs the book; faithful to her argument.
counterclaim_summary: Vendors report improved demographic accuracy since earlier audits.

claim_as_stated: OpenAI and Microsoft unlawfully copied millions of Times articles to train models that compete with and can reproduce Times content.
accuracy_rationale: graded: as a description of the filed allegation vs the complaint; faithful. (Truth of the allegation is for the court.)
counterclaim_summary: OpenAI argues transformative fair use; verbatim regurgitation is a rare edge case.

claim_as_stated: Training an LLM on books can be transformative fair use, but acquiring copies via piracy is not.
claimant: Judge William Alsup / authors (Bartz et al.)
accuracy_rationale: graded: as a description of the ruling vs the order; faithful to the partial holding.
counterclaim_summary: Ruling was partial; pirated-copy use exposed liability; later reported settlement.

claim_as_stated: Summary judgment for Meta on the specific record, with the judge warning the outcome was narrow.
claimant: Judge Vince Chhabria / authors (Kadrey et al.)
accuracy_rationale: graded: as a description of the ruling vs the order; faithful, including the judge's narrowness caveat.
counterclaim_summary: The judge stressed the ruling reflected the plaintiffs' weak showing, not a blanket endorsement.
notes: Ruling reportedly 2025-06-25.

claim_as_stated: Generative AI is built on uncompensated scraping of creators' work; creators deserve consent, credit, and compensation.
accuracy_rationale: graded: claim as made vs his stated position; faithful.
counterclaim_summary: AI firms argue training on public data is fair use and per-input licensing is impractical.

claim_as_stated: ChatGPT's data processing warranted a temporary block and later a fine over training-data lawfulness and age checks.
accuracy_rationale: graded: as a description of the regulatory action vs the record; faithful.
counterclaim_summary: OpenAI made changes to restore service and argues GDPR compliance.

claim_as_stated: Stability AI infringed by using Getty's images to train image models.
accuracy_rationale: graded: contested allegation vs final legal outcome; outcomes vary by jurisdiction and are not fully settled.
counterclaim_summary: Stability contests infringement and raises fair-use/territoriality defenses.

claim_as_stated: US data-center electricity use was ~176 TWh in 2023 (~4.4% of US electricity), projected to 325-580 TWh by 2028.
claim_source: 2024 US Data Center Energy Usage Report
accuracy_rationale: graded: LBNL's own statement vs its report; faithful and clearly scoped (US, all workloads).
counterclaim_summary: Not a counterclaim; the authoritative baseline. Projections carry wide uncertainty.

claim_as_stated: US data centers were responsible for 40% of the world's power demand last year - 313 terawatt-hours.
accuracy_rationale: graded: the post's wording vs the real figures; internally incoherent (313 TWh is ~1% of world power, not 40%) and misstates referents (data-center power->world power; US->global).
counterclaim_summary: Real figures: US ~176 TWh (2023); global data-center ~415 TWh (2024, ~1.5% of world); US ~45% of GLOBAL data-center electricity.
notes: Exact post date not confirmed.

claim_as_stated: Global data-center electricity could reach ~945 TWh by 2030 (base case), more than doubling, driven substantially by AI.
accuracy_rationale: graded: base-case projection vs outcome; a 2030 model output, not yet testable. Faithful to the report.
counterclaim_summary: IEA notes efficiency gains and the ~1.5% current share.

claim_as_stated: AI has a significant fresh-water footprint for cooling; per-session/per-query water use is non-trivial.
accuracy_rationale: graded: claim as made vs the paper; faithful, but per-query figures were later revised down by the authors and vary widely by site.
counterclaim_summary: Authors' own revisions temper per-query estimates; viral versions overstate them.

claim_as_stated: AI expansion is driving up tech-company emissions despite efficiency claims; Google's GHG rose ~51% from 2019 to 2024.
accuracy_rationale: graded: claim as made vs the disclosures; absolute emissions did rise, but the exact 51% figure vs 48% framing should be checked against the primary report.
counterclaim_summary: Companies cite clean-energy procurement and per-compute efficiency.
notes: 48% vs 51% flagged in verification; confirm against source.

claim_as_stated: A typical AI text query uses roughly 0.24-0.3 Wh (median), lower than some viral claims, though heavy queries use much more.
accuracy_rationale: graded: claim as made vs the Brookings synthesis; faithful, with the high-end caveat retained.
counterclaim_summary: Aggregate scale still matters even if per-query cost is low.

claim_as_stated: LLM-assisted essay writing was associated with lower neural connectivity, weaker recall of one's own text, and 'cognitive debt'.
accuracy_rationale: graded: claim as made vs the study; faithful to the within-study finding, but 'cognitive debt' over-reaches a small, short, single-task preprint.
counterclaim_summary: Small sample (~54), preprint, narrow task; authors cautioned against over-interpretation.

claim_as_stated: Higher confidence in generative AI is associated with less critical thinking; workers may offload cognitive effort.
claim_source: 'The Impact of Generative AI on Critical Thinking' (CHI 2025)
accuracy_rationale: graded: claim as made vs the study; faithful to its self-reported, correlational findings.
counterclaim_summary: Self-report/correlational; offloading is not inherently harmful. Framed as a shift.

claim_as_stated: Generative AI can augment productivity and widen access to expertise, with the largest gains for lower-skilled workers.
accuracy_rationale: graded: claim as made vs the field study; faithful to the call-center results.
counterclaim_summary: Gains may come with deskilling/dependency over time; effects vary by task.

claim_as_stated: Mitigating the risk of extinction from AI should be a global priority alongside pandemics and nuclear war.
claimant: CAIS signatories (Hinton, Bengio, Altman, Hassabis, et al.)
accuracy_rationale: graded: as a rendering of the statement vs the text; faithful (it is a real, signed one-sentence statement).
counterclaim_summary: Critics argue existential framing distracts from present harms.

claim_as_stated: Left Google to speak freely about AI dangers; advanced AI could pose serious, possibly existential risks.
claim_source: New York Times interview and talks
accuracy_rationale: graded: as a rendering of his statements vs the interview; faithful.
counterclaim_summary: LeCun and others argue current systems are far from such capability.

claim_as_stated: Fears of imminent, uncontrollable superintelligent AI are overblown; current LLMs lack real world models.
claimant_role: Founder, AMI Labs (formerly Chief AI Scientist, Meta; departed Nov 2025)
claim_source: Public talks, interviews, posts on X
accuracy_rationale: graded: as a statement of his position vs his public record; faithful.
counterclaim_summary: Safety researchers counter that capability gains are fast and waiting for proof is risky.
notes: Diffuse across many statements. | 2026 UPDATE: role changed - left Meta Nov 2025, founded AMI Labs (world models), raised $1.03B Mar 2026. Position on LLMs/superintelligence unchanged and now financially staked.

claim_as_stated: LLMs are unreliable, hallucination-prone, and not on a direct path to general intelligence.
accuracy_rationale: graded: as a statement of his position vs his record; faithful, and partly borne out by observable model behavior.
counterclaim_summary: Others argue scaling and tool use overcame many earlier objections.
notes: Diffuse across many pieces.

claim_as_stated: Current AI investment may be a bubble, with capital expenditure outrunning demonstrated returns.
accuracy_rationale: graded: forward-looking market claim vs outcome; not yet resolved.
counterclaim_summary: Optimists argue buildout is justified by long-run adoption even if near-term ROI lags.
notes: Diffuse discourse.

claim_as_stated: LLMs stitch together training text without understanding, and their scale raises environmental, bias, and accountability harms.
accuracy_rationale: graded: as a statement of her restated position vs her record; faithful.
counterclaim_summary: Some researchers argue emergent capabilities exceed the 'parrot' framing.

claim_as_stated: AI will act as a "virtual biologist," autonomously driving hypotheses and experiments and compressing 50-100 years of biological and medical progress into 5-10 years (the "compressed 21st century").
accuracy_rationale: graded as-made vs real-world outcome; a forward-looking forecast (5-10 year horizon, not yet elapsed) about AI acting as an autonomous "virtual biologist," so it cannot be scored true/false yet. Narrower, already-realized instances of LLM-driven discovery are documented on this referent (DeepMind's FunSearch/AlphaEvolve, OpenAI's autonomous Erdős disproof) -- real evidence the general mechanism works, but they don't verify Amodei's specific claim about compressing decades of biological/medical science.
counterclaim_summary: Critics reviewing the essay argue the "virtual biologist" framing skips over wet-lab, regulatory, and real-world experimental bottlenecks that better models alone don't remove.
notes: Head/primary proponent for this referent's broad claim; exact publication day within Oct 2024 not pinned -- earliest third-party coverage found is 2024-10-16.

claim_as_stated: AI (LLMs) can now make novel scientific discoveries on their own.
accuracy_rationale: true in the narrow, verified, engineered cases on this referent (FunSearch, AlphaEvolve, AI co-scientist, OpenAI's autonomous Erdős disproof); misleading when generalized to imply a standalone LLM autonomously "does science" end-to-end -- the documented cases pair an LLM with automated search/verification or multi-agent tool use on a human-framed, checkable problem.
counterclaim_summary: Researchers note these are narrow, engineered pipelines on checkable problems, not general autonomous discovery.
verification_status: Diffuse; not a single verifiable statement
notes: No single canonical origin; representative of widely circulated framing rather than one claimant.

claim_as_stated: Today's large language models may already be conscious or have some form of subjective experience.
claimant: Various AI researchers and lab executives (no single firm proponent identified)
claim_source: Public statements, 2022-2026 (see referent references for individual instances)
accuracy_rationale: graded as a general position vs the referent's authoritative_statement (Butlin et al. 2023: no current system meets consciousness indicator properties under any established theory; no agreed empirical test exists). No single claimant was found who flatly asserts "LLMs are conscious" as a firm, general claim: the most-cited instances are either explicitly hedged (Sutskever's 2022 "may be ... slightly"; Anthropic/Kyle Fish's 15-20% probability estimate, 2025-2026) or, in the one unhedged case (Lemoine on LaMDA, 2022), specific to a single chatbot and rejected by Google and the field. Rated premature/unverifiable rather than true or false on either side.
counterclaim_summary: Most AI researchers and cognitive scientists hold that current LLMs are not conscious under any established scientific theory (Butlin et al. 2023); Google rejected Lemoine's specific claim outright.
counterclaimant: Butlin et al. (2023 survey authors); Google (official statement on LaMDA)
verification_status: No firm as-made assertion of the general claim found; individual documented statements vary widely in strength/hedge -- see referent references
notes: Deliberately generalized rather than pinned to one head claimant -- see docs/prds/claims-proponent-display-prd.md for the open question of how to represent 'head vs. supporting' claimants in future UI.

claim_as_stated: ChatGPT uses 500ml (a bottle) of water per prompt/query.
accuracy_rationale: graded: circulating form vs the paper (v1/v5). Source says 500ml per ~20-50 Q&As (v1) / ~10-50 medium responses (v5) — i.e. ~10-50 mL per response; the per-prompt form is a 10-50x inflation. Also conflates scope (on-site cooling is 0-7.6 mL; the rest is off-site power-generation water) and freezes a GPT-3-era estimate.
counterclaim_summary: Author Shaolei Ren has publicly maintained the figure was misread as per-prompt; operator figures are far lower (Altman ~0.32 mL avg, Google 0.26 mL on-site median), each with its own boundary caveats.
notes: Merged 2026-07-05 from provenance register row water-500ml-per-prompt. Pairs with C028 (as-made) — the gap between them is where the distortion lives.

claim_as_stated: 'The median Gemini Apps text prompt uses 0.24 watt-hours (Wh) of energy, emits 0.03 grams of carbon dioxide equivalent (gCO2e), and consumes 0.26 milliliters (or about five drops) of water.'
accuracy_rationale: graded: as-made vs the disclosure itself; faithful — states median, text-only, and publishes both measurement boundaries (0.24 comprehensive / 0.10 chip-only).
notes: Merged 2026-07-05 from provenance register row gemini-energy-per-prompt.

claim_as_stated: A Gemini prompt uses 0.24 Wh of energy.
claim_source: Secondary coverage of the Google disclosure
accuracy_rationale: graded: circulating form vs the disclosure. The figure is real (comprehensive boundary) but circulation drops: MEDIAN not mean; TEXT prompts only; Gemini Apps only; May-2025 snapshot (energy fell 33x the prior year); and that the same source publishes 0.10 Wh chip-only — 'the' Gemini number depends entirely on which boundary is quoted.
notes: Merged 2026-07-05 from provenance register row gemini-energy-per-prompt.

claim_as_stated: 'The average query uses about 0.34 watt-hours... It also uses about 0.000085 gallons of water; roughly one fifteenth of a teaspoon.'
accuracy_rationale: graded: as-made vs available evidence; the claim is the only source for itself — no methodology, model mix, or measurement boundary disclosed, so it cannot be graded true/false against independent evidence. Epoch AI's independent ~0.3 Wh estimate is consistent but assumption-driven.
notes: Verified = the quote is verbatim from the fetched primary; the underlying figure remains unverifiable. Merged 2026-07-05 from provenance register row openai-energy-per-query.

claim_as_stated: A ChatGPT query uses 0.34 Wh of energy.
claim_source: Secondary coverage of the Altman post
accuracy_rationale: graded: circulating form vs the source. Same unverifiable core as C045, further stripped: drops 'average' and 'about', presents a hedged blog assertion as a measured fact, and implies a defined measurement boundary that was never disclosed.
notes: Merged 2026-07-05 from provenance register row openai-energy-per-query.

claim_as_stated: Companies cited AI as a reason for 54,836 announced US job cuts in 2025 (~5% of the total) and 101,743 in the first half of 2026 (~23%), making AI the leading stated reason for 2026 cuts.
accuracy_rationale: graded: as-made vs Challenger's own published reports; faithful — their posts state announced cuts, US employers, reasons from company statements.
notes: Merged 2026-07-05 from provenance register row ai-layoffs-challenger-counts.

claim_as_stated: AI caused ~55,000 layoffs in 2025; AI is the leading cause of 2026 job cuts.
accuracy_rationale: graded: circulating form vs Challenger's reports. The counts are real but the framing converts announced US cut PLANS with a company-stated reason into realized, global, verified AI causation — and drops the denominator (AI was ~5% of 2025 announced cuts).
counterclaim_summary: AI washing: companies blame AI for cuts they would make anyway (Altman, Feb 2026); Oxford Economics (Jan 2026) finds firms 'don't appear to be replacing workers with AI on a significant scale'.
notes: Merged 2026-07-05 from provenance register row ai-layoffs-challenger-counts.
